1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and reaches the standard 3.Nc3 set-up by a different move order. White keeps every plan open, from a broad pawn centre to a fianchetto, and Black decides whether to challenge the centre at once or to build a classical structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.strategy: Answers the fianchetto in kind: the bishop on g2 shelters the king and bears down on the long diagonal. Because e4 would block that bishop, White often avoids it and keeps the centre flexible, playing for a slower, patient fight instead of a big pawn centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3.background: Viktor Korchnoi was once its most notable practitioner, and it is one of the most popular lines at grandmaster level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.b4.strategy: An offbeat flank advance that grabs queenside space and clears b2 for the bishop. The pawn on b4 stands undefended and does nothing for the centre, so Black can complete development calmly and ask White to justify the loosening.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.b4.name: King's Indian Defence: Santasiere Variation

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O.strategy: Castles into the shelter of the fianchettoed bishop, so the king is safe at once. Black commits to no pawn structure yet and keeps the choice between a classical set-up and a direct strike at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares the classical structure, with the pawn on d6 holding the e5 square for a later central break. It usually transposes to the main line once Black castles, but it gives up the immediate central strike with the d-pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once from the wing, before castling. It is active, but d4 is defended twice and the king is still in the centre, so White can calmly continue development and Black's pawn move has no concrete follow-up.
